newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Eurobourses end down, depressed by Wall St.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurobourses end down, depressed by Wall St.

text.p: European bourses ended the day down on Wednesday, depressed by a revival of interest rate worries and a poor opening on Wall Street.
But French stocks and the franc clawed back some losses amid signs of progress in resolving the 10-day-old truckers' blockade, which has been slowly strangling the French economy.
The dollar was up over half a yen in late European trade after a Bank of Japan report on manufacturing pointed to no increases in interest rates, helping to support the U.S. currency.
French shares were in the doldrums for much of the day as investors fretted over the nationwide truckers protest but recovered to end only 4.31 points down at 2270.77 as hopes rose of a settlement.
The optimistic mood, however, was cut short when Wall Street made hefty losses at the opening because strong U.S. durable goods figures revived fears of inflationary pressures.

The stronger-than-expected demand for costly manufactured items in October wiped 0.5 percent off Wall Street as European bourses were closing. New York's drop followed a record-breaking run in recent days.

The franc, which weakened to 3.3926 to the mark because of the blockade, perked up as striking truckers and bosses made progress on key demands in marathon negotiations on Wednesday. The franc strengthened to 3.3890 marks in late trading.
Government mediator Robert Cros said the two sides had reached agreement on two central demands -- on early retirement and shorter hours.

London, Europe's biggest bourse, ended down after Wall Street's fall. "There is a feeling the Wall Street may have a wobble tonight though we've been thinking that for some time," said the head of sales trading at one brokerage.
London sentiment was also dented by the latest trade figures, which showed British exports were doing well despite strong sterling, raising concerns over inflationary pressures.
Investors had largely shrugged off rising interest rate expectations following Tuesday's budget but the new trade data saw inflation fears creep back.

The FTSE 100 index closed down 19.2 points at 4,049.2. After the market's surge to a record high ahead of the budget, strategists said that finance minister Kenneth Clarke's budget was conservative but not tight enough to allay pressure for further higher intererest rates.

In Frankfurt, floor trading ended down 0.5 percent after closing at a new peak on Tuesday. Carmaker Volkswagen AG tumbled six percent after a U.S. judge denied VW's motion to dismiss racketeering claims by rival Opel.
The dollar climbed against the yen as the Bank of Japan's quarterly Tankan report showed only a modest economic recovery and pointed to no change in interest rates.

"There is enough in this survey to confirm that the recovery continues...But it is perhaps less positive than I would have liked with interest rates on hold for the foreseeable future," said Daiwa Europe economist Julian Fisher.
But trading was thin ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday and the latest U.S. figures had little impact on the currency.

"The orders data were a bit strong and while we might see some more short-term (dollar/mark) gains, we tend to see the dollar rally running out of steam soon," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
CURRENCIES
The dollar was quoted at 113.33 yen and 1.5275 marks in late European trading against 112.65 yen and 1.5251 marks on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares ended 19.2 points lower at 4,049.2.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index finished down 4.31 at 2,270.77.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed down 13.61 at 2,797.03.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed unchanged at $373.75 an ounce after quiet trade ahead of U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. Silver ended at $4.74, down one cent.
